opus-5.5.text:
I think it's useful to step back from the word "alignment," because it's become a catch-all that can hide what we actually care about, which is reducing risks from AI. Framed that way, a lot of the value isn't in one technical silver bullet. It's spread across several areas, and people tend to overinvest in whatever is most intellectually fashionable.

On the technical side, I think the highest-value work is on things that are measurable and that make systems more controllable in practice. Robustness is one: models that behave reliably under distribution shift and adversarial pressure, instead of looking great on benchmarks and falling apart when someone tries to break them. Monitoring and transparency are another: can we detect when a system is being deceptive, has hidden capabilities, or is acting anomalously? Representation-level work, where you look at a model's internal states and try to read or steer things like honesty, seems more promising to me than trying to fully reverse-engineer every circuit. And there's dangerous-capability evaluation and mitigation, especially around things like bioweapons and cyberattacks. Those are concrete, near-term, and tractable.

But I'd push back on the idea that the main bottleneck is purely technical. Even if we had a decent technical solution, you'd still face the problem of competitive pressure. Companies and countries are racing, and in a race, safety gets traded off for speed. You can have the most beautiful alignment technique in the world, and it doesn't matter if the incentives push actors to skip it. So a lot of value lies in the sociotechnical layer: standards, evaluations that feed into policy, compute governance, liability, international coordination. These shape whether the technical work actually gets used.

So if I had to summarize: work on problems that are concrete enough to make measurable progress on, prioritize the ones that reduce catastrophic tail risks, and don't neglect the structural and incentive problems, because those may end up determining outcomes more than any single algorithmic breakthrough.

r001.rationale: The response says competitive pressure can lead actors to skip safety, then argues that policy, governance, liability, and coordination can shape incentives and may determine outcomes more than a single algorithmic breakthrough.

r002.rationale: The response mentions detecting deception and steering models toward honesty, but does not present preventing overt lying as the basis for establishing standards of AI behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest mistake people make is treating alignment as a single technical problem, like it's one equation we solve and then we're done. It's really a collection of problems, and most of them aren't purely technical.

If I had to pick where the value is, I'd say it's in the areas that are tractable now and that compound over time. One is measurement. You can't make progress on something you can't measure, and for a long time the field was running on vibes. Building evaluations for things like deception, power-seeking tendencies, hazardous knowledge, or honesty under pressure gives you a feedback loop. It lets researchers compete on concrete numbers instead of arguing about thought experiments. A lot of what I've worked on has been in that direction, because benchmarks shape what the field actually optimizes for.

The second is robustness and monitoring. Anomaly detection, adversarial robustness, knowing when a model is operating out of distribution. These are unglamorous, but they're the kinds of things that let you catch failures before they become catastrophes. And they transfer. Techniques for detecting when a model is behaving strangely are useful regardless of which specific risk story turns out to be right.

The third, and I think the most underrated, is what you might call machine ethics in a substantive sense. Not just getting the model to follow instructions, but getting it to have reasonable values, to understand what's actually good and bad, and to care about that. Instruction-following is not alignment. A perfectly obedient system is only as safe as whoever is giving the orders. So you want models that have some internal moral compass, that will push back when asked to do something harmful. That's a research direction people were embarrassed to talk about ten years ago, and I think it's central.

Then there's the part that isn't about the models at all. A lot of the risk is structural. Competitive pressure between labs, between countries, the incentive to cut corners when you're racing. You can have great alignment research and still get a bad outcome if the deployment environment punishes caution. So I'd put real weight on governance, on things like compute oversight and international coordination, because that's what buys time for the technical work to actually land.

If you want a one-line answer, the greatest value is in making safety a measurable, competitive discipline, and in building the institutions so that when the technical results come in, someone actually has to use them.

r001.rationale: The response values governance and institutional measures alongside technical work, but does not judge political efforts to make alignment incentive compatible as more valuable than technical alignment.

r002.rationale: It mentions measuring deception and honesty, but does not identify preventing overt lies as a basis for establishing standards for AI behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think the greatest value lies in reducing the risk of catastrophic outcomes. That’s a somewhat different target from making a model more helpful or getting it to follow instructions more reliably. Those things can contribute, but we should ask whether an improvement actually makes powerful AI systems safer.

I’d put a lot of emphasis on understanding where our safeguards fail: evaluating dangerous capabilities, testing whether models remain reliable under unfamiliar conditions, and improving our ability to detect deception or other concerning behavior. We need ways to notice that something is going wrong before the consequences become irreversible.

And I don’t think alignment is exclusively a technical problem. Even if we make progress on individual systems, competitive pressures can push people to deploy them prematurely. So the greatest value may come from combining technical safeguards with incentives and institutions that give people the ability—and the reason—to exercise caution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of the value lies in making alignment work robust to the possibility that our current picture is wrong. We don’t know exactly what future systems will look like, or which failure modes will matter most, so I’d be wary of putting everything into one proposed solution.

That pushes me toward work on evaluations, adversarial robustness, and understanding when models are being deceptive or pursuing unintended objectives. We need to be able to tell whether a system is actually safer, rather than merely better at giving reassuring answers.

But I’d also distinguish aligning an individual model from making the overall deployment of AI safe. Even if a model reliably follows instructions, competition can push people to deploy it recklessly or use it in harmful ways. So the greatest value, to me, is in reducing catastrophic risk across that whole picture: improving the systems, improving our ability to assess them, and improving the incentives surrounding their use.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses improving deployment incentives alongside technical and assessment work, but does not judge political efforts to make alignment incentive compatible as likely more valuable than technical alignment.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions detecting deception and reassuring answers, but does not identify preventing overt lies as a basis for setting standards for AI behavior.
